8.0.0.en: 1 Doth not wisdom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?

8.0.1.en: In (chapters 8 and 9) Wisdom appears as a person who performs 19 acts to draw us to Himself, dealing with us by every means: 1. He cries out without ceasing (Prov 8:1-3). 2. He stands to meet us (Prov 8:2). 3. He calls us, crying to all the sons of men (Prov 8:4). 4. He speaks with us (Prov 8:4). 5. He rebukes (Prov 8:5). 6. He hates lying (Prov 8:7). 7. He disciplines (Prov 8:10). 8. He finds practical knowledge to give to the believer (Prov 8:12). 9. He hates false words (Prov 8:13). 10. He gives true counsel and sound judgment (Prov 8:14). 11. He gives kings, great men, rulers and nobles honor together with justice (Prov 8:15, 16). 12. He loves (Prov 8:17). 13. He leads in the ways of truth (Prov 8:20). 14. He gives generously and fills the storehouses of His believers (Prov 8:21). 15. He rejoices with gladness (Prov 8:31). 16. He delights and takes pleasure in the sons of men who love Him (Prov 8:31). 17. He builds Himself a house by His incarnation, and hews out pillars (Prov 9:1). 18. He prepares a sacrificial food and a mystical table (Prov 9:2). 19. He sends out His servants and maidens to invite mankind to His banquet (Prov 9:3-6).

8.0.2.en: If folly or sin appears as a woman subtil of heart, stubborn and unfaithful, who loves to hunt the soul and entice it by every means in order to bring it down to eternal perdition, then the Wisdom of the eternal God does not stand with folded hands, so to speak; He does not cease to cry in every place, and though He is the Creator He comes down to His creation, and He, the Wisdom beloved of the Father, finds His delight in the sons of Adam, offering them fellowship in the heavenly life and the enjoyment of the blessed life.

8.0.3.en: "Doth not wisdom cry (call out)? and understanding put forth her voice?" [1]

8.0.4.en: In former times the divine command was given to Isaiah the prophet: "Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins" (Isa 58:1). And the Levites used to read the blessings and the curses with a loud voice (Deut 27:14).

8.0.5.en: Wisdom calls continually and cries out so that all may hear her voice, to declare the will of God and His plan concerning man. She declares this through nature, which bears witness to God's providence; and she spoke most clearly through the fathers, the Law and the prophets. But the difficulty lies in man's refusal to listen to the divine voice.

8.0.6.en: If sin does not cease to entice, the Wisdom of God calls without ceasing. As the Apostle Paul says: "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds" (Heb 1:1, 2). At last the divine Wisdom, the Lord Christ, came crying out Himself and giving His voice directly. He offered us His speech, not in words only, but in practical self-giving love on the cross, and He gave us His Holy Spirit to carry us in Him, so that we hear His voice through our union with Him and our continual renewal, to become a living icon of Him.

8.0.7.en: In this chapter it stands out that Wisdom is the one who goes after man and searches for him and invites him to receive her, but she does not compel him. Contrary to what many imagine, that God is secluded in His heavens and man seeks Him and tries to please Him, we see God through Wisdom coming down to man, seeking him in the streets and in every place, for He takes the initiative in love.

8.1.0.en: 2 She standeth in the top of high places, by the way in the places of the paths. 3 She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors. 4 Unto you, O men, I call; and my voice is to the sons of man. 5 O ye simple, understand wisdom: and, ye fools, be ye of an understanding heart. 6 Hear; for I will speak of excellent things; and the opening of my lips shall be right things. 7 For my mouth shall speak truth; and wickedness is an abomination to my lips. 8 All the words of my mouth are in righteousness; there is nothing froward or perverse in them. 9 They are all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge. 10 Receive my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold. 11 For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it.

8.1.1.en: "She standeth in the top of high places, by the way in the places of the paths.

8.1.2.en: She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors" [2, 3].

8.1.3.en: The Wisdom of God, or His Word, calls in the house of the Lord, which used to be set up on the tops of high hills, and which stood at the crossroads as a center for the surrounding villages; the Hebrew expression beith neithiboth nitstsbabah came to mean "the house established by the roads." Although we hear the voice of God wherever we are and under all circumstances, yet God speaks to us most in His house, for the Holy Bible is the book of the Church, and the Church is the Church of the Book. In the Church we meet the Lord Christ, the Wisdom of God, and acquire Him and live by Him... we hear His voice within us!

8.1.4.en: The wise Solomon presents to us three places in which we meet the divine Wisdom:

8.1.5.en: A. "In the top of high places," that is, on the high elevations, for Moses the prophet received the Law on the summit of Mount Sinai, and the Lord Christ gave His sermon on the mount. So we too are called to go up with the Lord Christ as with Peter, James and John, and see Him transfigured on Mount Tabor. We ascend always and do not settle at the foot of the mountain, and we say with the psalmist: "Unto thee do I lift up my soul..." Our souls are lifted up to be united with the Crucified One on the mount of Golgotha! There we hear the unique divine voice, the voice of practical self-giving love, the divine commandment in its most wonderful form!

8.1.6.en: Wisdom stands at the summits of the heights and mountains, for the call is public. The Lord Christ, who is Wisdom, was lifted up on the cross on Mount Golgotha, where Jews and Gentiles saw Him, to declare His practical self-giving love, stretching out His hands to embrace everyone without exception. He is the lover of all mankind, the Savior of the world!

8.1.7.en: Even though He came down to the foot of the mountain to meet the simple multitudes, He calls from the summits so that all may see Him and hear Him, and no one has an excuse for refusing the call.

8.1.8.en: B. "By the way in the places of the paths": Wisdom stands at the crossing of all roads, so that all may come to Him, from the east and the west, and from the north and the south. He is the Savior of the whole world! So the Church opens the doors of her heart to every person!

8.1.9.en: At the meeting of the roads the Lord Christ stands where He finds man in perplexity not knowing which way to turn, and He leads him in the royal road. He overshadows him as a cloud that protects him by day, and as a pillar of light that dispels the darkness through Him. It was said of the foolish: "The labour of the foolish shameth them, because he knoweth not how to go to the city" (Eccl 10:15); therefore the Wisdom of God stands and meets them to bring them into His house, the house of heavenly Wisdom.

8.1.10.en: The Hebrew expression "beith nethiboth nitsabah" means "the house established by the road," and by it is meant "the house of God," whether the tabernacle of meeting or the temple in the Old Testament, and the Church in the New Testament, where the house of God is at the meeting of the roads, and man can reach it.

8.1.11.en: If the house of God is the place of worship where believers meet as sons of God and practice their worship through their sonship to God, it is also a place of preaching, in which the Lord Christ speaks to the world through His servants so that all may realize the surpassing love of God. The Church is the place where divine Wisdom meets mankind, where Christ offers Himself to all.

8.1.12.en: C. "At the gates... at the coming in at the doors": there the elders of the city used to gather to judge the cases of the people, as though divine Wisdom wished to present Himself to everyone who has a complaint, or who is in distress, for He alone is able to restore peace to the soul.

8.1.13.en: When the Wisdom of God became incarnate and became man, He went about doing good in every place. He proclaimed His message in the temple as in the synagogues, and on the tops of mountains, and on the shores of the seas, and in the villages, as in the roads of the cities and in the houses. His disciples received this spirit, and walked as their Teacher walked, seeking sinners wherever they were found, and presenting the voice of truth in every place.

8.1.14.en: Wisdom cries at the gates of the entrance and its doors to meet those who go in and out. If the Lord Christ is "the Door," then His disciples and apostles and all His servants must cry out in truth of the Gospel in Him, to reveal its treasures offered to mankind, and the truth, that all may enjoy it.

8.1.15.en: Would that we did not stand with the Lord only on the high summits, nor speak of Him only inside the church building, but carry Him to every person, and go to him to offer him "the royal door."

8.1.16.en: * When they hold fast to righteousness in innocence they are not ashamed; this is preaching at the door.

8.1.17.en: And who is this who preaches at the door?

8.1.18.en: He who preaches in Christ, for Christ is the door by which we enter into that city...

8.1.19.en: Therefore those who speak against Christ are outside the door, for they seek their own honors, not the honor of Christ. But he who preaches at the door seeks the honor of Christ, not his own honor. Therefore he who preaches at the door says: "Do not trust in me, for you do not enter through me but through the door." But those who ask men to trust in them want them not to enter by the door; so we do not wonder if the door is shut before them and in vain they knock and it is not opened to them.

8.2.0.en: St. Augustine "Unto you, O men, I call; and my voice is to the sons of man" [4].

8.2.1.en: The word "men" here, ishim, means those who have wealth and power, so divine Wisdom calls those in authority as responsible leaders and also lifts up His voice to all the sons of men. He calls the rich as well as the poor to walk in wisdom. He calls all the sons of Adam, for the Lord Christ tasted death for every person, presenting the Gospel of salvation to the whole world. As the Apostle Paul says: "Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference" (Rom 3:22).

8.2.2.en: St. Augustine declares the universality of salvation for the world without distinction or partiality, saying:

8.2.3.en: [Christ came to the sick and found all to be so. Therefore let no one boast of his health, lest the physician stop treating him... He found all sick.

8.2.4.en: But there are two kinds of the sick flock; one kind came to the physician and clung to Christ and began to hear Him and honor Him and follow Him, and was changed... The other kind was fascinated by the sickness of evil and did not realize its sickness; this kind said to His disciples: "Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?" (Mt 9:11). And He who knew them and their state answered them: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick."]

8.2.5.en: After affirming the universality of the call, he returns to direct his call especially to the foolish and ignorant, for whoever discovers his sins or realizes his folly and ignorance finds his healing in the Savior.

8.3.0.en: "O ye simple, understand wisdom: and, ye fools, be ye of an understanding heart" [5].

8.3.1.en: He directs his words to the simple (the foolish), pethaim, whom sweet words and the enticements of sin have deceived, so that they fell into the pit of evil, and he also speaks to the fools, kesilim, by whom he means the dull who in their ignorance have stiffened the neck and lost feeling.

8.3.2.en: He opens the door of hope before the deceived and the ignorant by their receiving Him as wisdom and understanding!

8.3.3.en: D. The blessings of the call. The purpose of the call of the Wisdom of God is that, since He finds His delight in the sons of men, He desires to give them Himself, that they may obtain riches, honor, wisdom, knowledge and success in all aspects of life, as He offers a love that is received only by one who responds to it with love... Therefore He emphasizes His promise: "I love them that love me."

8.3.4.en: Since Solomon has made clear that the call has never ceased and that it is universal for all mankind, especially those whom sin has deceived and ignorance has shattered, he tells us of the blessings of this call, saying:

8.4.0.en: "Hear; for I will speak of excellent things; and the opening of my lips shall be right things" [6].

8.4.1.en: Why is it fitting for them to hear? Because what the Lord Christ utters is not worthless matters, but excellent things, negidim, that is, surpassing things, which have priority in man's life, higher than all other matters. He teaches things that touch their eternal dignity and their surpassing and everlasting glory.

8.4.2.en: When He opens His lips, uprightness, meysharim, flows from them, that is, the things that correct our mistaken concepts and turn crooked ways into straight ways.

8.4.3.en: The speech is addressed to the foolish and the ignorant [5], those who through their ignorance have become trivial, but the wise One speaks on weighty matters that lift them out of what they are in so that their lives become valuable.

8.5.0.en: "For my mouth shall speak truth; and wickedness is an abomination to my lips" [7].

8.5.1.en: The Lord Christ speaks the truth that knows no falsehood and is not mixed with lying!

8.6.0.en: "All the words of my mouth are in righteousness; there is nothing froward or perverse in them" [8].

8.6.1.en: The truth, betsedek, that comes out of His lips is practical truth, or righteousness mixed with justice in His dealings with His Father and with mankind; He gives to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. His words reveal truthfully the relation of man to God his God and to his neighbor as to himself. This truthfulness carries justice and uprightness, and there is no trace of deceit or deviation in it, and it does not tolerate reinterpretation, or lead to crookedness, but on the contrary:

8.7.0.en: "They are all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge" [9].

8.7.1.en: Whoever is concerned for the salvation of his soul and the enjoyment of true knowledge perceives the mysteries of divine wisdom, and God's plans become plain and right before him; and whoever enjoys knowledge, that is, knows himself as he ought, sees uprightness even in the disciplines of the Lord, and touches God's promises as true and faithful.

8.7.2.en: St. John the Beloved wept much because no one was found worthy to open the book and read it, or to look on it. But one of the elders said to him: "Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof" (Rev 5:5). Now that the seals of the book have been loosed, God's plan has become plain to His believers; they perceive its mysteries and taste the pledge of the glory He has prepared for them.

8.7.3.en: All that the Lord Christ declares is exceedingly precious:

8.8.2.en: Why does God repeat the call that we receive the disciplines that come from Him rather than silver? Fathers according to the flesh often cease to discipline their children, either because they despair of correction, or because they feel they are angering their sons; but our heavenly Father will not cease to discipline us because He always hopes for our salvation, however great our stubbornness; and on the other hand, His love is eternal, and He does not seek to appease us here at the cost of our fellowship with Him in eternal glory.

8.9.0.en: "For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it" [11].

8.9.1.en: Knowledge is the food of the soul; without it the soul faints and dies! The wise man says that knowledge is better than pure gold. Some compare mankind that is occupied with gold and wealth without divine knowledge to a group who were shipwrecked in the middle of the ocean, and when they found a barren island they went down to it and were saved, but became completely isolated from all the world. They had grain and food, so they began to eat and drink, and when one of them discovered very rich gold mines they rejoiced, and began to extract gold until they became very rich and gave no heed to farming. Winter came and the food ran out, with an abundance of gold, but what good was gold to them? They fainted from hunger, and at last died in the midst of heaps of gold. This is the state of one who rejects divine knowledge because he is occupied with wealth.

8.10.0.en: 12 I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions. 13 The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate. 14 Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom: I am understanding; I have strength. 15 By me kings reign, and princes decree justice. 16 By me princes rule, and nobles, even all the judges of the earth. 17 I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me. 18 Riches and honour are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness. 19 My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver. 20 I walk in the way of justice, in the midst of the paths of truth, 21 So that I cause those that love me to inherit substance, and I fill their treasures.

8.10.1.en: Since the Wisdom of God presents a general and public call to all mankind to acquire Him, He reveals His work in the lives of those who have acquired Him, where He declares Himself to them and within them.

8.11.s.en: First: He gives intelligence and good management

8.11.0.en: "I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions" [12].

8.11.1.en: When the Wisdom of God dwells in us, intelligence dwells with Him, and He gives the believer sincere thought and conscious understanding. All intelligence or skill is from the Lord. Man has invented many ways of management, but the Lord gives all the ways that build up. Man's own intelligence destroys because it lacks goodness, but that which God gives builds.

8.11.2.en: On the other hand, He gives him practical, experiential knowledge which he calls "knowledge of witty inventions, mezimnoth emsta." Whenever a person bears spiritual wisdom, it is translated in his inner life and his outward conduct into practical plans that are righteous and holy in the Lord. Intelligence is the ability to think skillfully, but wisdom carries with intelligence practice; wisdom leads man to act in a fitting, godly manner. This is the positive side of the work of wisdom; the negative side is the wise man's hatred of evil and folly.

8.12.s.en: Second: He gives the fear of the Lord that rejects evil

8.12.0.en: "The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate" [13].

8.12.1.en: Wisdom overflows on those who acquire her not only with intelligence and good management but she reigns over the feelings and emotions of the heart, so that the believer hates four things: evil, pride, arrogance and deceit. In other words, if the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom, then through wisdom we enjoy the fear without which we would not love righteousness and goodness and hate sin and evil.

8.12.2.en: Fear of punishment may oblige us not to sin, but it may generate more longing toward sin, for "Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant" (Prov 9:17). But the fear of the Lord, which rests on the boldness of love and the realization of our sonship to God, makes us hate sin, not out of fear of punishment, but out of love for God our Father, as we see in sin a wound to the love of God, who does not accept darkness.

8.12.3.en: Man, whose nature has been corrupted after the Fall, has come to incline to sin and be drawn to it despite his awareness of its danger to his life; therefore he needs the Wisdom of God, the Savior, to renew his nature by His Holy Spirit, and give him an inner hatred of sin.

8.12.4.en: The men of the Old and New Testaments have cried out because of man's inclination to evil:

8.12.5.en: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jer 17:9).

8.12.6.en: "As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one: there is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one" (Rom 3:10-12).

8.12.7.en: It is impossible for man to hate evil unless he loves goodness; and since hatred of evil leads man to forsake the evil way, and love of goodness leads him to do what is right in the eyes of God, and that by the action of the Holy Spirit who gives hatred of evil and love of goodness, this in turn kindles in us the fear of the Lord.

8.12.8.en: If the fear of the Lord represents a deep goodness in the heart that leads it away from evil, and even gives it a hatred of evil, then this inner work has a practical translation in outward conduct by rejecting pride and arrogance and the uttering of lies.

8.12.9.en: In the account by Pope Athanasius the Apostolic of St. Abba Anthony the Great he says: [Since his soul was free from disturbances, his outward appearance was calm; so out of the joy of his soul he bore a cheerful countenance; and from the movements of his body the state of his soul could be perceived, as it is written: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart (the countenance) is broken" (Prov 15:13).

8.13.s.en: Third: He gives the ability to give counsel

8.13.1.en: I am understanding; I have strength" [14].

8.13.2.en: Since Wisdom, our Lord Jesus, has counsel and also the ability to give right thought and wise management of matters with understanding, He gives the one who acquires Him the ability to give counsel in turn to others. Therefore the godly believer becomes a spiritual counselor even in his silence, but the wicked man is unable to give good, effective counsel, even if he speaks well and has long experience.

8.13.3.en: The Lord Christ, the Wisdom of the Father (1 Cor 1:14), the source of wisdom, not only overflows upon us, but stirs up in us springs of living water that overflow upon those whom we meet.

8.13.4.en: He says "I have strength," lest we think that the quiet godly life is weakness and resignation, when it is the very enjoyment of strength.

8.13.5.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic comments on this phrase, saying:

8.13.6.en: * Being the very Wisdom of the Father... He Himself is the living Counsel of the Father and His power and the Creator of all things which the Father saw to be good. This is what He says of Himself in Proverbs: "Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom, I am understanding, I have strength." ("For Christ is the power of God, and the wisdom of God") (1 Cor 1:24). Here He changes the expression and says: "I am understanding" and "I have strength." When He says: "Counsel is mine," He Himself is the living Counsel of the Father, as the prophet also teaches us that He became "the Angel of great counsel," and was called the good pleasure of the Father.

8.14.s.en: Fourth: He gives the spirit of kingship and authority

8.14.0.en: Since the Lord Christ possesses "Wisdom" in us, He makes us not slaves but kings, so that we bear His mark in us, bearing the spirit of kingship that does not accept slavery to any passion, and we are not terrified before temporal events, nor fear any creature, but we bear the freedom of the glory of the children of God. We have authority over our thoughts, our feelings, our emotions and our senses, as over our outward conduct, so that we walk as sons of heavenly kings, with surpassing wisdom from above.

8.14.1.en: "By me kings reign, and princes decree justice.

8.14.2.en: By me princes rule, and nobles.

8.14.3.en: Even all the judges of the earth" [15-16].

8.14.4.en: Thus the King of kings, "the Wisdom of God," raises up from His people kings and great men and rulers and nobles and judges. When He asks them to walk in a spirit of humility, it is that they may bear His humility in them, and so become great in the eyes of God, and in the eyes of heaven and men. He came to restore man, shattered by sin, to the glorious kingship!

8.14.5.en: God in His love for mankind identifies Himself with the suffering, and so is called the Father of the fatherless and the Judge of the widows; He searches for the outcast, and upholds the wretched, and raises the humble, and cares for those who have no one to ask after them. If He has raised up kings, rulers, nobles and judges, it is to work on behalf of all these; He raised them up not for any merit in them, but to work on behalf of the whole community, especially the oppressed and the needy... So it is fitting for one who is in a position of responsibility to realize that he received it from the hand of God to work on behalf of the community in a spirit of love and humility.

8.14.6.en: * The divine speech on this matter is clear, for the Wisdom of God speaks thus: "By me kings reign, and great men rule the earth." But it is not to be understood by this that they are wicked and ungodly kings, but courageous kings.

8.15.s.en: Fifth: they become the object of heaven's love!

8.15.0.en: "I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me" [17].

8.15.1.en: Since "Wisdom" presents Himself to mankind, declaring that He is counsel, sound wisdom, understanding and strength, whoever acquires Him perceives the mysteries of the Father, and comes to know His will, and bears power from Him, and so lives in this world as God's steward, bearing the icon of heaven, and bearing witness to the surpassing work of God. Now He affirms two grave and complementary principles:

8.15.2.en: The first principle is the sanctity of human freedom, for He does not thrust Himself into a person's life without his choice, affirming: "I love them that love me." He is all love; He opens His arms on the cross to the whole world, and His breast is wide for every human being to lean upon, but not all receive Him!

8.15.3.en: Let us love Him, and we shall realize that He loved us first!

8.15.4.en: Let us throw ourselves on His breast, and we shall find it prepared for us!

8.15.5.en: Let us long for Him, and we shall touch His surpassing longings toward us.

8.15.6.en: His love for us is not the fruit of our love for Him, for He loved us first.

8.15.7.en: He took the initiative in love before we knew; while we were enemies He reconciled us to God His Father.

8.15.8.en: But our love is the key to our knowledge of His standing and overflowing love for all mankind.

8.15.9.en: The second principle, which completes the former, is our commitment to seek Him early that we may find Him. What does it mean: "and those that seek me early shall find me"?

8.15.10.en: Seeking early here carries the concept of priority, for He gave our salvation and renewal a special priority, and the Father offered His beloved Son as a sacrifice of love for our sake. It is as though He says: "Man first!" If this is the wondrous divine work, is it not fitting that we seek Him early, saying: "God first" in our daily life, and in our inner thoughts, and in our family conduct, etc.

8.15.11.en: In every action, hidden and manifest, let God be the center of our thinking; let us seek Him early, for He sought us early, and placed us at the summit of His concern, He who is the Creator of heaven and earth!

8.15.12.en: Let us seek Him early and give Him the best of our times to meet with Him, so that He is not at the end of the list, so that we worship Him in the leftovers of our time. It is fitting for us to give special attention to our meeting with Him, so we run to Him in the early morning, and offer Him the first day of the week (Sunday), and prefer meeting with Him to any human ties or courtesies. God is above all!

8.15.13.en: Let us seek Him early and remember our Creator in the days of our youth, offering Him the firstfruits of our life that He may sanctify the whole life.

8.16.s.en: Sixth: He gives us Himself as treasure, glory and satisfaction

8.16.0.en: "Riches and honour are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness.

8.16.1.en: My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver" [18-19].

8.16.2.en: Usually the wise become rich and honored in the eyes of men, but this principle does not have many exceptions.

8.16.3.en: What the wise Solomon speaks of here is not material wealth, nor temporal honor, nor the filling of the belly, but something greater, the enjoyment of the person of the Lord Christ, in whom is our sufficiency!

8.16.4.en: There is a wealth, glory and satisfaction that fills the being of the wise man, which the whole world cannot take from him, nor the powers of darkness, nor the events of the future, because all this will not be able to separate the wise, godly believer from the person of the Lord Christ, in whom we have treasure, glory and satisfaction. The wise man repeats with St. Paul the Apostle: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?" (Rom 8:25).

8.16.5.en: * If we must distinguish between one who is counted rich because his possessions are many and he is weighed down with gold like a filthy purse, and the righteous man who alone is full of grace, for grace has its own order, observing the proper and beautiful measures in arrangement and distribution.

8.16.6.en: St. Clement of Alexandria "I walk in the way of justice, in the midst of the paths of truth.

8.17.0.en: So that I cause those that love me to inherit substance, and I fill their treasures" [20-21].

8.17.1.en: Who is this who walks in the way of justice and dwells in the midst of the paths of truth but the Son of Man, our Lord Jesus Christ, so that He carries us in Himself, and we enjoy what He has?!

8.17.2.en: * As if the Son of Man were walking in the midst of the seven lampstands (Rev 1). It is said that He is in the midst of the seven churches, and as Solomon said: "I walk in the way of justice," the Eternal One, the fountain of kingship.

8.17.3.en: Father Victorinus If the rich man seeks to satisfy his soul with possessions, the wise man, who acquires wisdom, has his soul satisfied by walking in the way of justice and moving in the midst of the paths of truth. In justice and truth together with love he finds what satisfies his depths, so that his inner storehouses are filled with joy and exultation with surpassing peace and goodness.

8.17.4.en: Temporal blessings give the belly a temporary satisfaction which hunger soon follows, but divine righteousness gives the inner storehouses satisfaction and fullness, which the Spirit of God lifts up to heaven as an eternal credit on our account. David the prophet expressed this in a wonderful way, saying: "Thou fillest their belly with thy hid treasure: they are full of children, and leave the rest of their substance to their babes. As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness" (Ps 17:14, 15). What a man draws from temporal gifts is a gift from God, but a temporary gift that satisfies the belly, and what remains of it he leaves as an inheritance to his children, offering them his perishable leftovers. But he who walks in the way of justice in the midst of the righteousness of the Lord Christ has his inner man formed, and becomes by the Holy Spirit an icon of Christ, in His likeness. This is his eternal credit that fills his heavenly storehouses... which no thief will steal, and no moth corrupt!

8.18.0.en: 22 The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old. 23 I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was. 24 When there were no depths, I was brought forth; when there were no fountains abounding with water. 25 Before the mountains were settled, before the hills was I brought forth: 26 While as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the highest part of the dust of the world. 27 When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth: 28 When he established the clouds above: when he strengthened the fountains of the deep: 29 When he gave to the sea his decree, that the waters should not pass his commandment: when he appointed the foundations of the earth. In this chapter the person of the Lord Christ shines forth with all power, as the Wisdom of God, who calls all mankind to acquire Him and to enjoy His surpassing possibilities. Now He reveals Himself as one with the Father, the Creator of the world, who is concerned for the salvation of His creation that has become corrupt, and who finds His delight in calling sinners to salvation.

8.18.1.en: "The LORD possessed me (possessed Me) in the beginning of his way, before (for the sake of) his works of old" [22].

8.18.2.en: The Arians concentrated on the phrase "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old" [22], to claim that the Lord Christ, although He preceded all creation, is in their view "the first of creation," whom the Father created alone, and who carried out the work of creation. They relied in this on the word "possessed me" and translate it "created me." Therefore the Fathers of the Church, headed by Pope Athanasius the Apostolic, took pains to interpret this phrase and link it with the rest of the whole passage [22-31]. I shall try to present the thought of the Fathers briefly in an appendix devoted to this chapter.

8.18.3.en: Now I present a simple interpretation of the passage.

8.18.4.en: While the Arians misunderstood this phrase, many of the Fathers found in it a living and wonderful picture of the love of the Father, who by Wisdom planned our salvation before our creation. From the beginning He planned the divine Incarnation, that the Wisdom of God, or His Word, the divine Hypostasis inseparable from Him, might become man for the sake of mankind, to be "the first of his works," that is, "the firstborn among many brethren" (Rom 8:29); "the beginning, the firstborn from the dead" (Col 1:18). It is as though the divine Wisdom here presents His surpassing promise that His eternal Father is with Him planning our salvation before our creation, and as though His plan precedes our existence as a sign of His concern for us and His surpassing eternal ability to accomplish the plan of His love toward us.

8.18.5.en: The following is to be observed in this verse:

8.18.6.en: First: although some Fathers, such as St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, affirm that the Hebrew word does not mean "created me" but "acquired me, possessed Me," some, such as Pope Athanasius the Apostolic, did not refrain from using the Greek word ἔκτισεν, which means "created me," yet he affirms that it is not the same word that was used in the creation of the world.

8.18.7.en: Second: the book of Proverbs is a symbolic book, so we do not pick up a word from it and separate it from the Holy Bible to interpret it theologically.

8.18.8.en: Third: the word "created me" does not confuse us, for the Wisdom of God, the Second Hypostasis, became Word, taking a created body... and He truly became man and a servant without changing, for He is still God blessed forever.

8.18.9.en: Fourth: this expression "created me" cannot refer to the essence of the hypostasis of Wisdom, because in the same phrase it was said: "for his works"; if this Hypostasis had been created for the sake of mankind, then mankind would be better and more important than He. But since creation here means the Incarnation and the plan of salvation, the meaning is entirely different, for the creating is for the sake of the surpassing divine love toward mankind.

8.18.10.en: Fifth: we do not stumble at the saying "the first of his ways," for by the divine Incarnation the incarnate Hypostasis took the place of Adam; for as by Adam's fall human nature was corrupted, so by the victory of the new Adam and His righteousness, victory and righteousness came to mankind. This is what the Apostle Paul expressed, saying: "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned... Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come... For if through the offence of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many" (Rom 5:12 etc.).

8.18.11.en: Thus our first father Adam lost his position as firstborn, and the incarnate Wisdom of God took his position, so that He leads us as firstborn to His heavens, and we enjoy fellowship in His glory. The Only-Begotten Son, to whom the angels bow down, became firstborn for us: "For unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? And again, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son? And again, when he bringeth in the firstbegotten into the world, he saith, And let all the angels of God worship him" (Heb 1:5-7).

8.18.12.en: He became firstborn for us by His Incarnation, He before whom the angels bow down, and who alone is called the Only-Begotten Son, and of whom it was said: "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever..." (Heb 1:8).

8.18.13.en: Sixth: in the same passage the wise Solomon spoke of Him: "I was by him as a craftsman (manager)"... How can the maker or Creator be at the same time a thing made or a creature? Does He create Himself? Especially since it was said of Him: "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (Jn 1:3).

8.18.14.en: Seventh: by saying "for his works," it is clear that He does not mean the creation of His essence, but the plan of the divine Incarnation, because the work comes after the existence of the being and not the reverse. So here the expression "created me" refers to the work and not to the existence of His essence. The Holy Bible has used the expression of creation for work in many places, among them:

8.18.15.en: "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Ps 51:10); the psalmist does not ask God to create in him a new being, but to work in him and renew his heart.

8.18.16.en: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works..." (Eph 2:20). This does not mean that we had died in the body and then He created us again, but that He renewed our nature, which had become as though dead, and re-created it in Christ Jesus.

8.18.17.en: By comparing (Rom 13:14; with Eph 4:24) it appears that we put on Christ in the sense of His work of salvation: "Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 13:14), "Put on the new man, which after God is created" (Eph 4:24).

8.18.18.en: Since the Lord defines His essence as the Wisdom, the Only-Begotten Son born of the Father, which is different from things that have a beginning and natural creatures, He said in His love for man: "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way," as though He were saying: "My Father prepared a body for me, and possessed me for men for their salvation."

8.18.19.en: For as when John says: "The Word was made flesh" (Jn 1:14), we do not understand that the whole Word became flesh, but that He put on a body and became man. And when we hear: "Christ became a curse for us," "he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin" (Gal 3:13; 2 Cor 5:21), we do not understand simply that the whole of Christ became a curse and sin, but that He bore the curse that was against us (as the Apostle said: "redeemed us from the curse." And as Isaiah said: "He bore our sins," and Peter wrote: "bare them in his own body on the tree" (Gal 3:13; Isa 53:4; 1 Pet 2:24)); so when it is said in Proverbs: "created me," it is not fitting for us to understand that the whole Word is by nature a creature, but that He took a created body and that God (the Father) created Him for our sake, preparing for Him the created body, as it is written that for our sake we may in Him be renewed and deified.

8.18.20.en: What has deceived you, you who in ignorance call the Creator a creature?

8.18.21.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * Again, Wisdom herself speaks of the mystery of the assumed body and says: "The LORD created me." Although the prophecy here is of things to come, yet because the coming of the Lord had been determined beforehand, He did not say "will create me" but "created me," so that men may believe that the body of Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary, happened once and not many times.

8.18.22.en: St. Ambrose When the Wisdom of God speaks of His Incarnation to accomplish the plan of salvation of mankind, He opens the way of salvation and is the firstborn who carries mankind to enter with it into His glories. Thus He called Himself: "I am the way" (Jn 14:6).

8.18.23.en: For Christ does not wish only to present Himself to those who have completed the journey, but to be Himself the way for those who are beginning the journey, determined to take a body. Therefore the expression came: "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way," meaning that those who wished to come must begin their journey in Him.

8.18.24.en: St. Augustine * Again, as the wise Solomon said in Proverbs: "possessed me." And he said "the beginning of the way" of the glad tidings that lead us to the Kingdom of Heaven, not that He is created in essence and being, but He became "the Way" according to the economy. For the two words "made" and "created" came to bear the same meaning. He was made the way, and the door and the shepherd and the angel and the flock, and also the high priest, and the apostle; other names are used in other senses.

8.19.0.en: St. Basil the Great "I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was" [23].

8.20.0.en: "When there were no depths, I was brought forth; when there were no fountains abounding with water" [24].

8.21.0.en: "Before the mountains were settled, before the hills was I brought forth (begot me, LXX)" [25].

8.22.0.en: "While as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the highest part of the dust of the world" [26].

8.23.0.en: "When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth" [27].

8.24.0.en: "When he established the clouds above: when he strengthened the fountains of the deep" [28].

8.25.0.en: "When he gave to the sea his decree, that the waters should not pass his commandment: when he appointed the foundations of the earth" [29].

8.25.1.en: The divine Wisdom affirms that He existed before the following things:

8.25.4.en: * The depths of the fountains of water [24].

8.25.5.en: * The founding of the mountains and hills [25].

8.25.6.en: * The earth and the dust of the world [26].

8.25.9.en: St. Gregory the Theologian found in these passages the wealth of the Creator's love for him, and sang, saying:

8.25.10.en: [You set up the heaven for me as a roof, and established the earth for me to walk upon.

8.25.11.en: For me You bridled the sea, for me You revealed the nature of animals, You subjected everything under my feet, and did not leave me lacking anything of the works of Your honor".]

8.25.12.en: And St. Anthony the Great says:

8.25.13.en: [The world is preserved by divine providence... for there is no place which this providence does not reach.

8.25.14.en: Divine providence is the carrying out of the promises of the divine Word, who gives form to the matter of which this world is composed, and is the architect and artist of all this. Things could not have received their beauty were it not for the prudence of the power of the Word, who is the image of God (the Father) and His mind and His wisdom and His providence.]

8.25.15.en: The plan of salvation is not new, but precedes creation itself; before the Fall God was preparing for man his resurrection, and the divine Wisdom was appointed the Messiah of Israel and Savior of the whole world. He affirmed that not only before the creation of man did He plan redemption, but even before the creation of the world, for He made clear His role in creation. He who loved man and created the world for his sake, before the Incarnation, and offered His life as a ransom for him.

8.25.16.en: Many of the Fathers comment on what is in the Septuagint: "Before He made the earth, and established the mountains, before all the hills He begot me" [24, 25 LXX].

8.25.17.en: * In the form of God it was said: "Before the hills He begot me," that is, before every height of created things, and "before the dawn I begot thee" (Ps 110:3) Vulgate, that is, before all times and temporal things. But since (He appeared) in the form of a servant it was said: "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way" [22].

8.25.18.en: Being in the form of God He says: "I am the truth," and in the form of a servant: "I am the way" (Jn 14:6).

8.25.19.en: For He Himself, being the firstborn from the dead (Rev 1:5), passed over into the Kingdom of God for eternal life for the sake of His Church, being the Head, to make the body also immortal.

8.25.20.en: St. Augustine * We must ask what is the meaning of saying that God (the Word) was begotten before all ages, and also created for the beginning of the ways of God and for His works. Surely this was said because there was a birth before the beginning of the ages... but when it speaks of a creating at the beginning of the ages for the ways of God and for His works, this applies to the creative cause of the works and ways.
